claim: Alavizadeh et al. use risk as a metric of MTD effectiveness (placed defender-side in the table).
quote:
we utilize four security metrics – namely, sys-
tem risk, attack cost, return on attack, and reliability – to assess the effectiveness of the combined MTD tech-
niques
locator: abstract, p. 1772 (printed; PDF p. 1); defined Sec. III-D.1
issue: Use as an effectiveness metric holds (body Sec. III-D says the same: 'to evaluate the security of the cloud after deploying MTD techniques'). The defender-side placement is the table's frame; the source does not classify risk by side, though it defines risk on the network's components, which fits.

claim: Alavizadeh et al.'s mitigation factor is a defender-side MTD effectiveness metric.
quote:
Another evaluation measurement that uses the ALE values
of the cloud before and after deploying the MTD techniques
is the mitigation factor . The mitigation factor, denoted by
MFm, shows the ability of the defensive MTD techniques to
impair the attack.
locator: Sec. V-D, Eq. 13, p. 1782 (printed; PDF p. 11)
issue: The source presents the mitigation factor in Section V, 'Economic metrics for MTD techniques', as a benefit-of-security measure on annual loss expectancy (expected financial loss), not among its security metrics. 'Ability ... to impair the attack' supports an effectiveness reading, but the effectiveness placement is the table's, against the source's own grouping.

claim: Alavizadeh et al. use attack cost as an attacker-side efficiency metric.
quote:
AC measures the dif ﬁculties attackers face in
attacking a system, and can be quanti ﬁed in terms of the costs
an attacker incurs when seeking to exploit a network compo-
nent or the whole system [43].
issue: Attacker-side holds (the attacker's cost). Efficiency does not come from this source: it lists attack cost among the four security metrics used 'to assess the effectiveness of the combined MTD techniques' (abstract) and keeps cost-to-defender in its separate economic section. The efficiency row is the table's frame; the citation supports only 'uses attack cost'.

claim: Alavizadeh et al. use return on attack (RoA) as an attacker-side metric of cost against benefit.
quote:
Return on attack ( RoA) is a security metric based on the
attacker’s perspective [16]. RoA quantiﬁes the costs of the
attack versus the bene ﬁts of the attack.
issue: Attacker-side and cost-versus-benefit hold. The source takes RoA from its ref. [16], so it is a user of RoA, not its origin; the row also cites cremonini2005, which is right for the origin. Same efficiency-versus-effectiveness framing caveat as attack cost.
